claims.text: Isothermal aging of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA causes selective intermetallic precipitation and localized Mg depletion.
The aging-induced intermetallic compounds preferentially nucleate and grow at grain boundaries or other interfaces.
Localized Mg depletion changes elemental chemical activities at the oxide/alloy interface.
Changes in alloy-element activities and availability at the oxide/alloy interface can change the composition of oxidation products.
Mg-depleted regions reduce the availability of Mg for MgO formation during subsequent high-temperature oxidation.
Aging shifts the oxide scale from a predominantly MgO-based film toward a mixed scale enriched in Al2O3 or other stable oxides.
Al2O3 is a stable and potentially protective oxidation product.
The aging-induced mixed oxide scale is more protective than the baseline MgO-rich scale.
Thermally aged samples will oxidize more slowly than as-cast samples, as indicated by lower weight-gain kinetics.
Thermal aging will improve corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast baseline.
Stable intermetallic phases and passive surface oxides can impede corrosion-front propagation in Mg-containing alloys.
Corrosion in the cited Mg-containing alloys is governed principally by anodic Mg dissolution and the formation and partial breakdown of mixed oxide films.
The proposed initial material is an as-cast metastable Al-Mg-Cu-Zn-Gd-type HEA containing supersaturated solid-solution features and minor intermetallic content.
The as-cast baseline is initially homogeneous or only minimally segregated.
The as-cast baseline forms predominantly MgO-based surface films upon oxidation.
Non-equilibrium processing produces supersaturated solid solutions that are prone to diffusion-driven phase transformations.
The controlled comparison uses aging at 350 °C and 500 °C for 1–10 hours, followed by oxidation at 800 °C for 1–24 hours under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
An inert aging atmosphere is intended to isolate intrinsic diffusion-driven transformations from external contamination.
The comparison measures oxidation weight gain, oxide chemistry by in situ XPS, and intermetallic precipitation or compositional changes by SEM/TEM.
A lack of statistically significant differences in oxidation kinetics, oxide composition, or microstructural evolution between aged and as-cast samples would falsify the hypothesis.
